blocks.raw: <Callout variant="lea-watch">**LEA Diagnostic Clues for Post-Modernism:** On the exam, identify Post-Modern buildings by three visual giveaways: (1) Classical elements used ironically — broken pediments, oversized keystones, out-of-scale columns; (2) Playful or unexpected color — polychrome facades, pastel hues, neon accents; (3) Historical allusion mixed with pop culture — Chippendale tops, cartoon-like ornament, symbolic forms.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Example>**Vanna Venturi House (Robert Venturi, 1964):** The first built manifesto of Post-Modernism. A deliberately contradictory house in Chestnut Hill, PA with a split gable, oversized chimney, and distorted Classical references. Features: (1) Monumental gable facade — a "house-shaped" front that is purely symbolic, not structural; (2) A deliberate split in the gable line that contradicts the roof's own symmetry; (3) An oversized central chimney that dominates the composition.</Example>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>**LEA Trap:** "Post-Modernism means 'after Modernism' chronologically" — PARTIALLY TRUE but incomplete. Post-Modernism is a specific architectural movement defined by Venturi's Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966), not merely a temporal label. The movement is characterized by specific theoretical positions — historical allusion, double coding, irony, contextualism — that distinguish it from Late Modernism or any other "after Modernism" style.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <Warn>**Do NOT confuse Post-Modernism with Neo-Classicism.** Both use Classical elements (columns, pediments, arches), but Post-Modernism uses them ironically — out of scale, in unexpected colors, or in jarring combinations. Neo-Classicism uses them sincerely and proportionally. The Piazza d'Italia has neon-lit stainless-steel Corinthian columns — that is Post-Modern irony, not Neo-Classical reverence. The LEA tests this distinction directly.</Warn>

blocks.raw: <Tip>**Memory Anchor: "P-M = Post-Modernism = Pluralism + Metaphor."** Two defining characteristics: Pluralism (rejects the single "correct" style of Modernism — mixes historical references, ornament, color, and forms from different eras) and Metaphor (architecture communicates meaning through symbolism, allusion, and double coding — simultaneously appealing to popular taste and elite architectural culture).</Tip>
